summary:
We developed a data-driven method to identify Earth locations that measurably resemble the terrain of Mars and the Moon. Starting with nine lunar and Martian sites, we selected the northern mid-latitude polygonal terrain on Mars because high-resolution HiRISE imagery allows us to measure polygon size, geometry and evidence of shallow ice.

We evaluated Earth candidates using 12 weighted parameters, comparing topography, elevation, geology and terrain through NASA datasets, research papers and academic theses. The Changthang Plateau in Ladakh, India, ranked first, achieving approximately 92% similarity. We also documented differences that Earth cannot fully replicate, including atmospheric pressure, gravity and liquid meltwater.

Our project addresses the limitation of selecting analog sites based only on visual resemblance, replacing it with measurable scientific comparisons. We are also developing an interactive map, project website and demonstration video, which are currently under development.

Reliable Earth analogs allow researchers to test rovers, drills and resource-extraction technologies more safely and economically before actual lunar and Martian missions. Identifying new, less-studied locations expands research opportunities and supports future planetary base planning. Our interactive map will also make these findings accessible to students, educators and citizen scientists.

About Our Team

Mission Cosmos is brought together by a shared interest in space exploration, scientific discovery, technology and innovation. The team believes that the future of human exploration beyond Earth depends not only on technological advancement but also on understanding the environments in which future missions will operate.

The team combines scientific research, geographical investigation, data analysis, website development and visual communication. Rather than limiting research to familiar analog locations, it explores potentially overlooked environments and evaluates their scientific relevance through measurable characteristics.

 Project Demonstration

The website and demonstration video are being developed to communicate the project's objectives, scientific approach and intended outcomes.

●       Website: The main digital platform for presenting the research, explaining the comparison parameters, and exploring potential analog locations through an interactive map.

●       Demonstration Video: A visual introduction to the challenge, research approach, geographical comparison process, and intended applications.

Project Details

What the Project Does

Mission Cosmos identifies and compares Earth locations that share measurable geological and geographical traits with planetary environments, using NASA-provided data to examine topography, elevation, geology and terrain. It also examines differences, so that the limits of each analog are clear. Findings will be presented through an interactive map showing locations, the parameters compared and how Earth and planetary environments relate

Future Impact

Terrestrial testing cannot reproduce every extraterrestrial condition, but it can help in four ways:

●       Safer missions: Investigate terrain and geological challenges before deploying technology on planetary missions.

●       Lower cost: Run research and technology evaluation on Earth rather than relying entirely on expensive extraterrestrial testing.

●       Advancing Mars exploration: New analog locations widen the environments available for studying Martian terrain, surface materials, and exploration challenges.

●       Future human exploration: Supports work on habitat development, resource utilization, equipment, and environmental limits for lunar and Martian missions.

Where We Stand Out

Beyond Known Boundaries

We look past already-established analog sites to overlooked environments. Appearance alone is not evidence: two places can look alike yet differ in geological origin, surface materials or conditions. We rely on measurable characteristics and multiple comparison parameters.

Accuracy Through Multiple Sources

We use research papers, academic theses and NASA datasets together. Papers give background on formations and known analogs; NASA data supplies geographical and remote-sensing information. Comparisons rest on research and measurement, not assumptions.

From Discovery to Human Exploration

Potential research applications:

●       Rover testing: Terrain for mobility and navigation research.

●       Drilling technologies: Environments for subsurface exploration methods.

●       Resource investigations: Geology relevant to planetary resources.

●       Autonomous systems: Terrain challenges for autonomous navigation.

●       Habitat research: Geological and environmental factors for habitat planning.

We do not assume an Earth analog is a habitable planetary location. We ask what the comparison reveals, what further investigation is needed, and what engineering and protective systems human presence would require.

Team Integrity and Interactive Innovation

Instead of a long written report alone, the team will present the research as an interactive map and website that shows where potential analogs exist and why their characteristics matter.

“We don't just identify planetary similarities; we investigate their limitations, explore their possibilities, and transform scientific research into an experience that people can discover and understand.”

Mission Cosmos: Site Selection Analysis

Our team followed a progressive research-filtering approach. We did not select a location randomly. We gradually narrowed the candidates from nine planetary locations to four, then to one, and finally chose an Earth analog. At each stage we considered scientific research coverage, remaining knowledge gaps, data availability and, most importantly, the potential to identify a suitable Earth analog.

1. Initial Selection: 9 Locations

Our team first identified nine potentially interesting planetary locations: four on the Moon and five on Mars.

Moon: South Pole–Aitken Basin, Marius Hills, Gruithuisen Domes and Rima Sharp.

Mars: Northern Amazonis Planitia, Deuteronilus Mensae, Hellas Planitia, the Arabia Terra–Acidalia Planitia junction and Southern Utopia Planitia.

We wanted regions that:

•       Had scientifically interesting geological features

•       Could potentially support future human-base research

•       Had possible unresolved scientific questions

•       Could be compared with environments on Earth

2. First Filtering: 9 Locations → 4 Locations

In this first major selection stage, our team examined the existing research coverage and scientific uncertainties of the nine locations.

Locations eliminated

Our team eliminated eight locations in this stage. The South Pole–Aitken Basin was removed because it has extensive orbital research and a weak overlooked-site argument. Marius Hills was removed because of its well-known volcanic and lava-tube research. Gruithuisen Domes was removed because of active mission interest and substantial characterization. Northern Amazonis Planitia was removed because it has had recent detailed investigations. Deuteronilus Mensae was removed because of its established glacier and subsurface ice research. Hellas Planitia was removed because of extensive geological investigation. The Arabia Terra–Acidalia junction was removed because of existing habitat-suitability research, and Southern Utopia Planitia was removed because of its established exploration and research.

These locations were not rejected because they lack scientific value. Our team removed them because their general research topics or locations were already receiving considerable attention, which made our original overlooked-location objective less convincing.

Four locations retained

  1. Rima Sharp (Moon): possible underground lava-tube structures
  2. Rimae Mairan (Moon): possible underground volcanic structures
  3. Northern mid-latitude polygonal terrain (Mars): polygonal ground and possible subsurface ice
  4. Arcadia Planitia (Mars): subsurface ice and water-resource investigation

. Second Filtering: 4 Locations → 1 Planetary Location

This was the most important change in our selection strategy. Initially, our team was mainly looking for underexplored planetary locations. We then introduced an important additional requirement:

The planetary location must have sufficient existing scientific data to allow us to conduct a meaningful comparison with an Earth analog.

Instead of prioritizing only research gaps, we started prioritizing the ability to perform a proper scientific comparison.

Final Planetary Selection: Northern Mid-Latitude Polygonal Terrain, Mars

Our decision was driven by the ability to conduct a measurable scientific comparison. This location has extensive HiRISE observations and published geological investigations, and it contains measurable polygonal structures. This allows comparison of polygon size, shape, geometry, spacing, elevation and distribution.

The most important supporting evidence was:

  1. A 2024 study by Sako and colleagues examined approximately 4,789 HiRISE images across the 30°–42°N latitude band.
  2. It investigated different polygonal and periglacial landforms.
  3. Polygon dimensions and geometries can be measured using high-resolution images.
  4. Subsurface ice relationships can be investigated using available orbital evidence.
  5. Comparable polygonal terrain exists in terrestrial permafrost and cold-desert environments.

 

The study also identified a limitation: HiRISE covers only approximately 5% of its survey area, although broader, lower-resolution coverage is available.

Our final scientific reasoning was that this location:

•       Has enough existing planetary observations for research

•       Provides a scientific basis for comparison with Earth

•       Allows quantitative analysis instead of relying only on visual similarity

•       Leaves opportunities to discover and investigate a new terrestrial analog

Selection and Shortlisting Process (How & Why)

The identification of an optimal Earth analog followed a two-stage filtering framework—first isolating a specific Martian target from orbital data, and then evaluating terrestrial candidates against that target's physical, environmental, and resource-based criteria.

1.1 Establishing the Martian Reference Target

●       Orbital Image & Location Baseline: Anchored in Western Arabia Terra on Mars (coordinates 41.478° N, 6.132° E), within the 30° N–42° N northern mid-latitude periglacial belt, using Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) HiRISE image ESP_072398_2220.

●       Morphological Benchmark: 10–20 metre polygonal patterned ground displaying low-centred (LCP), high-centred (HCP), and transitional forms.

●       Subsurface & Resource Profile: A dry regolith lag (~0.2–1 m thick) overlying an ice-cemented permafrost table with shallow pore and segregated water ice (supported by neutron spectrometer and shallow radar data).

●       Environmental Constraints: Hyper-arid cold desert conditions, gentle regional slopes (< 3°–5°), high UV exposure, and active wind-driven dust and sand redistribution.

1.2 Shortlisting the Earth Analog (Changthang Plateau)

Using the Martian target as a baseline, three global terrestrial candidates were evaluated across 12 weighted parameters (covering polygon geometry, climate, subsurface ice, and in-situ resources): (1) Changthang Cold Desert Plateau (Ladakh, India), (2) Adventdalen (Svalbard, Norway), and (3) Qaidam Basin Margin (Qinghai, China).

●       Eliminating Svalbard (78% Match): Although Svalbard exhibits well-developed ice-wedge polygons (15–30 m), its maritime Arctic climate introduces high moisture, wet organic-rich peat soils, and heavy snow cover—variables that distort comparisons with hyper-arid, low-organic Martian regolith.

●       Eliminating Qaidam Basin (81% Match): While Qaidam offers an arid, high-altitude desert setting with 8–18 m desiccation/frost polygons, its permafrost is largely ephemeral rather than a sustained, ice-cemented permafrost table comparable to mid-latitude Mars.

●       Selecting Changthang Plateau (~92% Match): Situated in the Himalayan rain shadow at 4,530–4,800 m elevation, its flat basin floors (0°–4° slope) feature 10–22 m thermal contraction polygons (LCP and HCP) driven by extreme diurnal temperature swings (-30°C to +20°C) and intense UV flux. Crucially, beneath a 0.5–1.5 m dry active layer, it holds accessible subsurface water ice (~80 cm depth) alongside evaporite mineral deposits (borax, mirabilite, halite, gypsum) and basaltic/silicate regolith suitable for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) testing.

Why and How They Match vs. Diverge

●      Core Similarities (Why & How): Both sites share identical polygon diameters (10–22 m vs. 10–20 m) and 4-to-6-sided geometry because frozen sediments possess equivalent brittle-elastic tensile strength, and flat slopes (0°–5°) allow cooling stresses to propagate isotropically. Persistent winds trap mobile sand inside recessed cracks, driving parallel transitions from low-centred (LCP) to high-centred (HCP) relief.

●       Core Divergences (Why & How): In Changthang, summer warmth above 0°C enables liquid water percolation into cracks to form pure ice wedges. On Mars, ~6 mbar pressure sits below water's triple point, forcing polygons to evolve solely via solid-to-vapor sublimation and sand wedging. Additionally, Earth's higher gravity (1g vs. 0.38g) increases lithostatic confining pressure.

Irreproducible Objectives & Value for Future Scientists

●       Objectives That Cannot Be Reproduced on Earth: Field campaigns in Ladakh cannot physically replicate sub-triple-point CO2/H2O ice sublimation kinetics, 0.38g lithostatic overburden crack depths, winter CO2 frost condensation (-125°C), or complete abiotic sterility (due to native extremophilic microbes).

●       How This Research Helps Future Scientists: Correlating surface LCP/HCP relief with borehole ice depths (~0.8 m) and GPR profiles in Changthang enables inversion models to estimate subsurface water-ice volume on Mars directly from HiRISE imagery, while providing an accessible testbed for rotary-percussive ice drills, ISRU extraction, and biosignature preservation studies.
